summary:
Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring schools to seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, requiring parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and pausing third-party school programs. The policy was enacted as The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023, with the province invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause, a five-year override.

In Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 of 11 August 2025, the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision, holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches of the pronoun-notice policy where section 33 has been invoked, so the policy stands. The same ruling granted the government's appeal in part and held that a judge does have jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, so UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench.

Amnesty International Canada, an intervenor in the appeal, welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights, arguing that use of the override clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy, and noting that courts can still issue a declaration that the law violates the Charter even where the clause shields it from being struck down.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both the province and UR Pride asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy; the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before the country's highest court, and counsel for Egale Canada noted that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

Saskatchewan is one of three provinces, with British Columbia and Ontario, that will grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing a wider range of queer and trans families.
tangentialFactors:
Saskatchewan's use of the notwithstanding clause in 2023 is the mechanism that keeps the school consent rule out of reach of a strike-down; the province argued before the Court of Appeal that the clause should end the challenge entirely, and the courts rejected that argument while still leaving the policy in force.

The Supreme Court of Canada's agreement on 6 November 2025 to take the Saskatchewan appeal together with the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21, on a request for expedited hearing, places the province's school policy among the country's live constitutional cases.

Saskatchewan legalized same-sex adoption in 2001, one of the earlier provinces to do so.
localsOnly:
Residents who experience discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression in employment, housing, or accommodations have a complaints route under Saskatchewan's provincial human rights legislation.

Residents may change their legal gender under the province's own procedure, and Saskatchewan is one of three provinces granting parental status to three or more intentional parents, which affects recognition of trans and queer family structures.

For residents with children in the school system, the 2023 policy requires parental or guardian consent before a student under 16 may use a gender-related preferred name or pronouns at school, requires parental notification about the sexual-health curriculum, and has paused third-party school programs.

No Saskatchewan-specific provincial correctional rule or case governing the placement of gender-diverse prisoners is documented in the sources; provincial correctional policies vary and the inventory records none for Saskatchewan.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources characterize the 11 August 2025 Court of Appeal holding differently: one reports that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches where section 33 was invoked, so the policy stands; another reports that the appeal was granted only in part and that a judge retains jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights. Which Charter grounds survive, and on what basis, is unresolved in the inventory.

The outcome of the Supreme Court of Canada hearing is not documented beyond the 6 November 2025 announcement that the court will hear the appeals.

No trans-specific violence or homicide figures for Saskatchewan, and no Saskatchewan-specific survey of public attitudes toward transgender people, appear in the inventory; the neighbour-tolerance and social-acceptance polling available is national, not provincial, and is carried at the national layer.

No Saskatchewan-specific rule for the placement of gender-diverse people in provincial corrections is sourced; the question is unresolved at this level.
